subject: Exit policy assertion and proxy binding discussion for private endpoint
messages:
From: Andrew Cho <andrew@caduceuslabs.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood-inference.com>
Cc: security-engineering@caduceuslabs.com
Date: 2028-06-10T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private endpoint outbound constraints — control plane / proxy binding questions

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. As we start drafting our firewall policy for a private Redwood deployment, the security team has a few open questions we need answered before we can sign off:

1) Egress identity: do you support a static set of egress IPs for control-plane callbacks, or is the runtime ephemeral and requires us to allow an FQDN / proxy? We have a strict NAT policy and prefer allowlisting IPs but can consider proxy binding if it provides equivalent auditability.

2) mTLS / certificate validation: can Redwood present client certs to our proxy (or accept our proxy's client cert) for mutual TLS? We need cert thumbprints to pin in our proxy configuration and a rotation cadence.

3) SNI / FQDN expectations: if we allow via FQDN, what exact hostnames and SAN entries should we allow? Are there wildcard CNs?

4) Telemetry & evidence: for our procurement and SOC scope we need an evidence bundle showing outbound endpoints, TLS fingerprints, and example connection logs (redacted).

Can you point us to a short checklist we can hand to our networking team? If you have a diagram of the recommended proxy binding/egress architecture that would help.

Appreciate a concise list we can take to our firewall owners.

Thanks,
Andrew
Andrew Cho
Head of Infrastructure — Caduceus Labs

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood-inference.com>
To: Andrew Cho <andrew@caduceuslabs.com>
Cc: David Kim <david.kim@redwood-inference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood-inference.com>
Date: 2028-06-10T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint outbound constraints — control plane / proxy binding questions

Hi Andrew — thanks, great questions. I put together a short, actionable plan below and attached an evidence CSV and a simple diagram for your network team. TL;DR: we can support both static egress IPs (recommended for strict allowlist environments) and a proxy-binding mode that preserves auditability.

Summary / answers:
- Static egress IPs: For the control plane (callbacks, token introspection, telemetry), we can allocate a small set of static egress IPs for your tenant on Redwood Dedicated/Private. Example (placeholder): 34.201.112.45, 34.201.112.46, 34.201.112.47. If you require provider-owned IPs in your NAT table, we can formalize these in the procurement attachment and rotate only with prior notice.
- Proxy binding: If you prefer to route via your proxy, Redwood supports outbound proxy binding using a configurable SNI override and client certificate pinning. In this flow Redwood's runtime initiates TLS to your proxy; the proxy terminates and forwards to control-plane endpoints. We provide cert thumbprints and a short rotation API.
- mTLS: We support mutual TLS for control-plane callbacks. We can provide PEM-encoded client certs for Redwood-to-proxy auth or accept your proxy's client cert when Redwood validates inbound callbacks. We can provide thumbprints and a rotation schedule (90 days by default) and will coordinate before any rotation.
- Hostnames / SNI: Allowlist the following exact hostnames (used by control plane): api.redwood-inference.com, telemetry.redwood-inference.com, token.redwood-inference.com. We do not rely on wildcard CNs for control-plane; SANs include the exact hostnames above. If you prefer FQDN-only allowlisting, use those.
- Ports & protocols: TLS 443 outbound from the private runtime to the control plane / telemetry endpoints. Optional ports for healthchecks: 8080 from our ops probes (we can disable).
- Evidence bundle: attached egress-evidence.csv contains sample connection evidence (timestamp, egress-ip, dest-fqdn, tls-fingerprint). Also attached a proxy-binding-diagram.png. We can produce additional redacted logs if needed.

Action items / next steps:
1) Confirm whether you need static IPs or proxy-binding. If static IPs, tell us the NAT table owner and we will produce a signed IP-assertion artifact for procurement.
2) If proxy-binding, tell us the proxy TLS requirements (client cert pinning vs token introspection). We will provide cert thumbprints and an API for rotation notifications.
3) We will prepare an "egress PSM checklist" (attached) for your firewall team to run through and sign off.

Attaching: egress-evidence.csv, proxy-binding-diagram.png, egress-psm-checklist.pdf

Best,
Soojin Lee
Security Partnerships — Redwood Inference

From: Andrew Cho <andrew@caduceuslabs.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood-inference.com>
Cc: security-engineering@caduceuslabs.com, procurement@caduceuslabs.com
Date: 2028-06-10T11:09:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint outbound constraints — control plane / proxy binding questions

Hi Soojin — this is helpful, thanks. A few clarifying points from our side: 

- Static IPs: we generally avoid admitting third-party-owned IPs into our NAT table unless we have contractual guarantees around rotation and attestations. If Redwood can commit to a 30-day pre-rotation notice and provide signed rotation manifests, that helps procurement.

- Proxy binding: we'd prefer proxy-binding for our multi-tenant edge. Our proxy supports both client cert pinning and SNI-based routing; however we would need Redwood to support HTTP header-based token introspection as a fallback. Can you confirm if Redwood can include an X-Redwood-Tenant header or similar on outbound control-plane connections for correlation?

- DNS resolution: will the runtime resolve api.redwood-inference.com locally (i.e., inside our VPC) or will it rely on Redwood's DNS? We need to know for split-horizon setups.

- Evidence: please include a sample signed rotation manifest and an example TLS fingerprint (SHA256) for the current client cert in the bundle. Our GRC team will want to store that in the evidence repository.

If you can confirm the above, security can draft the final firewall guidance and procurement can proceed. One ask: can you also outline a short test plan we can run that validates both static-IP allowlisting and proxy-binding (5-10 minute checklist for our ops team)?

Thanks,
Andrew

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood-inference.com>
To: Andrew Cho <andrew@caduceuslabs.com>
Cc: David Kim <david.kim@redwood-inference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood-inference.com>
Date: 2028-06-10T15:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private endpoint outbound constraints — control plane / proxy binding questions

Andrew — great, below is a compact acceptance checklist and answers to your bullet points. I also sketched a 3-step test plan so your ops team can validate quickly.

Acceptance checklist (network/firewall owners):
- If static IPs chosen: add 34.201.112.45, 34.201.112.46, 34.201.112.47 to outbound NAT allowlist for tenant X. Only TLS/443 allowed to api.redwood-inference.com, telemetry.redwood-inference.com, token.redwood-inference.com.
- If proxy-binding chosen: configure proxy to accept inbound TLS from Redwood runtime and forward to control-plane. Allowlist proxy hostname(s) and install provided Redwood client cert thumbprint (SHA256: AA:BB:CC:...:11).
- mTLS: Enable mutual TLS on control-plane connections; pin certs via thumbprint; rotation cadence 90 days by default; Redwood will provide signed rotation manifests at least 30 days prior to rotation.
- Headers / correlation: We can add an X-Redwood-Tenant header on control-plane requests (configurable). If you require header-based token introspection, we support an introspection endpoint over TLS for token verification.
- DNS: The runtime resolves hostnames using the customer VPC DNS by default (split-horizon supported). If you prefer Redwood-managed DNS, we can discuss but most customers prefer VPC-resolved names.
- Evidence: we'll provide the sample signed rotation manifest (signed by Redwood PKI), the current cert SHA256 fingerprint, and a redacted connection log sample. See attached egress-evidence.csv (first two rows are sample) and the egress-psm-checklist.pdf.

3-step test plan for ops (10 minutes):
1) Static IP smoke (if chosen): temporarily add the three static egress IPs to your NAT table; run the Redwood healthcheck call from a staging runtime; validate connection established to api.redwood-inference.com and that the egress IP in logs matches.
2) Proxy-binding smoke (if chosen): point the staging runtime at your proxy; install the Redwood cert thumbprint on proxy; perform an authenticated token introspection request; verify X-Redwood-Tenant header present and logs show client cert pin.
3) Rotation validation: request a signed rotation manifest from Redwood support and verify signature + thumbprint match the cert presented during a connection.

If this looks good I will: (a) generate the formal IP-assertion artifact for procurement (if static IPs), (b) provide the signed rotation manifest draft, and (c) schedule a 30-minute ops handshake with your firewall team for tomorrow.
